hints: Focus on where the forward and reverse changes happen, heating below and reforming on the cold surface above.
Notice that heat is needed to break down the solid, so think about what that tells you about heat flow for reaction 1.
Ask yourself if a reaction can go backwards without being in dynamic equilibrium in the same closed container.
walkthrough:
**Check if the reaction is reversible**

Think simply: can it go forwards and backwards? Heating gives $\text{NH}_3$ + $\text{HCl}$, cooling gives back $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$.

$$\text{NH}_4\text{Cl(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_3\text{(g)} + \text{HCl(g)}$$

**Check if it is endothermic**

You have to keep heating the solid to make it decompose. That means heat is taken in to break the lattice.

$$\text{heat taken in, so } \Delta H > 0 \text{, endothermic}$$

**Check if it is in dynamic equilibrium**

Dynamic equilibrium needs a closed system where forward and reverse happen at the same time at the same rate. Here the gases move away and reform in a different, colder place, so it is not equilibrium.

So statement 1 is false, statements 2 and 3 are true.

options.A: States 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. Statements 2 and 3 are correct but statement 1 is wrong, so this combination fails. The trap is thinking any reversible reaction must be at equilibrium.
options.B: States 1 and 2 only are correct. Statement 2 is correct but statement 1 is wrong. Reversibility does not guarantee dynamic equilibrium in this open apparatus.
options.C: States 2 and 3 only are correct. The reaction is reversible because $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ reforms on cooling, and endothermic because heating drives decomposition. It is not in dynamic equilibrium because forward and reverse occur under different conditions in an open system.
options.D: States 1 only is correct. Statement 1 is actually false. Dynamic equilibrium requires a closed system with equal forward and reverse rates, which is not happening here.
